query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticle stability at high temperatures is governed by the limited atomic mobility imposed during low‐temperature synthesis combined with strong local anchoring to defects or edge sites on the support, which together prevent phase separation and coarsening despite high service temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized from solid mixed precursors under low-temperature reduction conditions, with minimal free atomic mobility.
generation.intervention: Modify the nanoparticle support to either enhance or diminish anchoring (for example, by engineering a support with an increased density of defective edge sites, such as turbostratic graphite edge planes, versus a smooth support with minimal defects).
generation.conditions: High‐temperature catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) service environments where atomic diffusion normally promotes phase separation or coarsening.
generation.structural_mediator: Strong nanoparticle–support interactions (anchoring at defect or edge sites) that physically restrict atomic movement in the nanoparticle lattice.
generation.mechanism: During synthesis, limited atomic mobility freezes in the high-entropy mixed state. When supported on a substrate with defect-rich features (e.g., T-graphite edge planes), nanoparticles are further stabilized by strong interfacial binding that retards atomic diffusion and segregation even under high thermal energy, thereby preserving the homogeneous single-phase structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles deposited on supports engineered for strong anchoring will show significantly lower rates of particle growth, phase segregation, or structural degradation under prolonged high-temperature operation compared to those on smooth supports with little anchoring.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized and deposited on standard, minimally defective supports (or in solution-based synthesis where atom mobility is less restricted) that show faster diffusion-mediated coarsening at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: This stabilization mechanism is expected to be effective primarily in systems where synthesis occurs far from thermodynamic equilibrium (limited atomic mobility) and where the support surface chemistry can be controlled. In synthesis methods where the precursors are fully mobile (e.g., high-temperature solution-based syntheses) the effect may be diminished.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contributions of the high configurational entropy versus support anchoring are not yet fully determined; additional factors such as specific interatomic mixing enthalpies may also play significant roles.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical multi-element HEA nanoparticles using a low-temperature solid precursor reduction method. Deposit one set on a support engineered to have a high density of anchoring defects (e.g., rough, edge-rich T-graphite) and the other on a smooth, inert support lacking such defects. Subject both sets simultaneously to in situ high-temperature annealing (using TEM heating) under identical controlled conditions.
measurements: Nanoparticle size distribution before and after annealing (via TEM imaging)
Phase homogeneity and elemental distribution (using in situ X-ray diffraction / X-ray absorption spectroscopy)
Onset temperature of observable coarsening or phase segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles on the anchoring-enhanced support do not show a statistically significant improvement in suppression of particle coarsening or phase segregation compared to the control sample on the smooth support, the hypothesis that strong nanoparticle–support interactions are the key factor in high-temperature stability will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This simple model of particle formation demonstrates that adding more elements innately promotes a more random nanoparticle, regardless of element interactions. Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways. AbstractDirect formation of ultra-small nanoparticles on carbon supports by rapid high temperature synthesis method offers new opportunities for scalable nanomanufacturing and the synthesis of stable multi-elemental nanoparticles. However, the underlying mechanisms affecting the dispersion and stability of nanoparticles on the supports during high temperature processing remain enigmatic. In this work, we report the observation of metallic nanoparticles formation and stabilization on carbon supports through in situ Joule heating method. We find that the formation of metallic nanoparticles is associated with the simultaneous phase transition of amorphous carbon to a highly defective turbostratic graphite (T-graphite). Molecular dynamic (MD) simulations suggest that the defective T-graphite provide numerous nucleation sites for the nanoparticles to form. Furthermore, the nanoparticles partially intercalate and take root on edge planes, leading to high binding energy on support. This interaction between nanoparticles and T-graphite substrate strengthens the anchoring and provides excellent thermal stability to the nanoparticles. Further in situ annealing studies up to 1173 K also confirms the excellent thermal stability of nanoparticles. We believe the mechanistic details reported in this work would not only guide the nanoparticles synthesis through Joule heating-based methods, but also pave the way on understanding other rapid high temperature synthesis approaches.
